newsitem.title: USA: Christopher urges continued Mideast momentum.
newsitem.headline: Christopher urges continued Mideast momentum.

text.p: Outgoing U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Wednesday urged Israel and the Palestinians to build on the momentum of their Hebron accord but said aid to the Middle East might have to be cut anyway if Congress continues to slash other assistance programmes.

"Aid to Israel, Egypt and Jordan will inevitably come under pressure, perhaps irresistible pressure, if our other assistance programmes continued to be decimated," he said. "The biggest crisis facing our foreign policy today is whether we will spend what we must to have an effective foreign policy."

Five days before he leaves office and returns to California, Christopher, whose designated successor Madeleine Albright is expected to be confirmed by the Senate next Tuesday, gave a final formal address at Harvard University's John F. Kennedy School of Government.

Hailing the Hebron deal he said: "Now that the parties have taken this difficult step, they must not step back in fatigue. They must now use this new momentum to move ahead to build the peace that is in the common interest of Israelis and Palestinians alike."

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, after months of haggling, clinched the accord at an overnight summit. It requires Israel to withdraw from 80 percent of Hebron in 10 days and implement the first of three other West Bank redeployments by March 7.
The Hebron deal was an ideological wrench for Netanyahu and his Likud Party, who had vowed never to cede any part of the biblical Land of Israel to Palestinians.

Christopher, who spent much of his tenure engaged on Middle East issues, said: "We must remember that we were able to help the parties reach their agreement because of our leadership and engagement -- and because we have had the resources to support those who took the risks for peace."

In another strong pitch for more foreign affairs spending, he warned that the United States had reached a point where "we cannot respond to a crisis in one part of the world without taking funds from valuable programmes in other regions."

To support U.S. military deployment in Haiti aid to Turkey had to be cut, and to monitor the ceasefire in northern Iraq the State Department "shortchanged" the peace process in Guatemala, he said without further explanation.

"If a new crisis occurred today we would have to make a choice: which long-term interest -- probably an already underfunded interest -- should be sacrificed to meet the short-term need," Christopher said.

He noted that U.S. aid programmes have declined by 37 percent in the last decade and "half of our bilateral aid now supports the Middle East peace process ... (which) advances a vital interest and must be preserved."

But if additional funds are not approved by Congress, he said, aid to Israel, Egypt and Jordan will come under pressure that could force reductions as demands grow for money to underwrite U.S. leadership in new crises.

His speech was part of a full-court press by the Clinton administration to win increased finding this year for the State Department and related agencies. U.S. officials say President Bill Clinton is expected to ask Congress this year for an extra $1.2 billion in foreign affairs funding, plus $1 billion to pay back dues owed to the United Nations.
Christopher did not confirm these figures but stressed that the need for U.S. leadership in the world is rarely questioned in the United States.
